1.grade_fit_note: 'finally' (dropping the doubled l in -ally) is a standard grade 4-5 word; easy end of grade 5.
1.note: 'finaly' should be 'finally'. The other sentences contain 'pieces', 'address' and 'probably', all spelled correctly, so they are reasonable lures.

2.grade_fit_note: 'answer' (silent w) is a grade 2-3 high-frequency word; the other sentences use only simple words, so the error stands out.
2.note: 'anwser' should be 'answer'. A, B and C have no word harder than 'studied'/'straight', so a grade 5 student has little to weigh against D.

3.grade_fit_note: Direction vs named region is a standard grade 5-6 capitalization point.
3.note: 'driving south' is a direction (lowercase); 'the Southwest' is a named US region (capitalized). The 2x2 design over the two words is clean.

4.note: 2x2 over eau/eu and -ful/-full. A sound item, just low for grade 5.

5.grade_fit_note: Proper adjectives (Victorian, Persian) are a grade 5-6 point.
5.note: Both are proper adjectives and are capitalized in all mainstream dictionaries. 'modern' works well as an uncapitalized control.

6.grade_fit_note: 'existence' (-ence vs -ance) suits grades 7-8; the distractor words 'harass', 'medieval' and 'mischievous' are good, hard lures.
6.note: 'existance' should be 'existence'. Strong distractors: harass (one r), medieval and mischievous are all classic misspellings, here spelled correctly.

7.note: 'truely' should be 'truly'. 'column', 'height' and 'foreign' are good, tricky lures.

8.grade_fit_note: 'privilege' is a classic grade 7-8 demon word.
8.note: 2x2 over vi/ve and -lege/-ledge. All three distractors are real, common misspellings.

9.note: 2x2 over m/mm and r/rr. The structure is fine but the word is low for grade 5.

10.note: 2x2 over c/cc and -ence/-ance; every option has rr, so the doubled-r rule is not tested.

13.note: 'commitee' should be 'committee'. 'conscious', 'miniature' and 'souvenir' are good lures.

14.note: 2x2 over the second and third vowels (i/e). Clean.

15.note: 2x2 over es-/ex- and -ally/-aly. The 'ex' lure matches a common real error.

16.grade_fit_note: Brand name vs generic product noun suits grade 6.
16.note: Capitalize the brand and lowercase the generic noun. A weak objection: if the fictional trademark were 'Sunny Day Sunscreen', B or D could be argued, but the sentence gives no sign of that, and treating both products the same way supports C.

17.note: 2x2 over hyp/hyph and the/thi. The 'hyph' lure is less natural but still plausible.

18.grade_fit_note: Title capitalization with a short verb ('Is') vs an article suits grades 5-6, at the harder end for grade 5.
18.note: In every mainstream title-case style, 'Is' is capitalized (it is a verb) and 'the' is lowercase. The trap of lowercasing the short word 'is' works well.

20.grade_fit_note: A common noun reused after a proper name suits grades 5-6.
20.note: 'the park' and 'the river' are common nouns here. Clean 2x2.

21.note: 'guarentee' should be 'guarantee'. 'conscience', 'hygiene' and 'possession' are strong lures.

23.note: 2x2 over ir/irr and -ible/-able. 'irresistable' is a very common real error, so C is a strong lure.

24.note: The distractors combine a missing n with an o/r transposition. All are natural errors.

25.grade_fit_note: 'surveillance' is hard but within reach for grade 8 (it could also sit at grade 9).

26.note: 'seperate' should be 'separate'. 'capital' is the correct word for a city, which makes it a good homophone lure. 'knowledge', 'business' and 'February' are also strong.

28.grade_fit_note: Family titles used as names vs after a possessive suit grades 4-5.
28.note: 'Grandpa' is used as a name and is capitalized. 'my uncle' and 'my grandmother' follow a possessive and stay lowercase. The 'Grandpa' control is well placed.

29.note: 'cemetary' should be 'cemetery'. 'apparent', 'sincerely' and 'valuable' are good lures.

30.note: 2x2 over the two unstressed vowels (e/a). It is a strong item, because the lures copy the verb 'maintain'.

31.grade_fit_note: Full quoted sentence vs an integrated quoted fragment suits grades 6-7.
31.note: A complete quoted sentence after 'told us,' is capitalized. A fragment blended into the sentence without a comma is lowercase. Clean 2x2.

32.grade_fit_note: Historical documents and events suit grade 5.
32.note: 'Bill of Rights' and 'American Revolution' are both proper names and are fully capitalized. Clean 2x2.

_batch.Spelling: I found no cross-item pattern that gives away the answer. All 16 word-completion items (4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 19, 22, 23, 24, 25, 27, 30) use a 2x2 design: two error sites, with the key as one cell and the three other cells as distractors. Each feature therefore splits 2-2 across the options, and neither 'majority feature' voting nor picking the option between the others can find the key. Option lengths differ by at most a letter or two in both directions. Keys by position: A 5, B 6, C 3, D 2. That is a mild under-use of D, not exploitable. The 8 error-in-sentence items (1, 2, 6, 7, 13, 21, 26, 29) have keys A, D, C, D, D, C, C, D: 7 of 8 are C or D, and 4 of 8 are D. Over a whole test, 'guess C/D' on this format would beat chance (about 87% vs 50% for the pair). That is worth rebalancing toward A and B. In the higher-grade sentence items the error word sits among correctly spelled hard words, which is good. In items 1 and 2 (grade 5) the distractor sentences are simple, so the error stands out in item 2 especially.
_batch.Capitalization: I found no cross-item pattern that gives away the answer. All 8 items (3, 5, 16, 18, 20, 28, 31, 32) use a 2x2 over two capitalization sites. Keys: D, B, C, A, C, B, D, A, exactly two per letter. The key pattern varies: both capitalized (5, 32), both lowercase (16, 20, 28), and one of each (3, 18, 31). So 'most capitals', 'fewest capitals' and 'the mixed option' each fail on several items. Within each item the options are the same length apart from case, so length gives nothing away.
